brief: Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok notes the US Gulf Coast diesel crack spread cleared $100 per barrel in August, a record high against a normal range of $15 to $30. Unlike a gasoline spike, which lands as a one-time tax on discretionary consumer spending, diesel is an intermediate input embedded in the delivered cost of nearly every physical good, including freight, rail, agriculture, and construction. Because of that structural difference, the diesel price rise does not stay in the energy line of the CPI but migrates with a lag into core goods and services, a pass-through the Fed cannot dismiss as transitory. The note's bottom line is that diesel margins are now setting the long end of the yield curve, because diesel crack spreads are an important driver of future core inflation.
